name: Watching a Switch Learn
brief:
Three PCs on one switch, one broadcast domain, no routers anywhere. A switch starts life knowing nothing: its MAC address table is empty until traffic teaches it. Your job is to watch that happen and be able to explain it afterwards.

Check the table before you send anything. Then ping, and check again.
watchFor: The first frame to an unknown destination gets flooded out every other port. That is not a failure, it is how learning starts.

tasks.text: On SW1, confirm the MAC address table is empty before any traffic.
Back on SW1, confirm the switch has now learned at least two MAC addresses.
tasks.hint: One entry for the sender on Fa0/1, one for the responder on Fa0/2.

tasks.text: On PC1, run `arp -a` and confirm PC1 learned PC2 hardware address.
tasks.hint: Because PC2 is on the same subnet, PC1 ARPs for PC2 directly rather than for a gateway.

tasks.text: From PC1, ping PC3 at 192.168.1.13 and watch a third entry appear.
Clear the dynamic entries on SW1 and confirm the table is empty again.
tasks.hint: `clear mac address-table dynamic`. Everything the switch learned is forgotten, and it relearns on the next frame.

extension: Predict, before you run it: after clearing the table, does the next ping from PC1 to PC2 succeed? Does the switch flood it? Run it and check whether your prediction held.
debrief:
A switch builds its table from source addresses, not destination addresses. It learns where a device is by hearing from it, which is why the table fills in as a side effect of traffic rather than as a configuration step.

In a competition topology, `show mac address-table` is how you confirm a device is really on the port you think it is on.
